fable-5.1.text:
It's genuinely one of the hardest questions to answer rigorously, and I want to be honest that we can't fully answer it.

The cleanest thing we can say is about the workflow, not the molecules. When we looked at what the agents converged on, the overall shape of the pipeline was recognizable to the human experts on our team. Structure-based modeling, then a scoring and filtering step, then iterative rounds of refinement with feedback. That's a fairly standard playbook in the field. So in one sense the answer is yes, a competent human team would likely have landed somewhere in the same neighborhood of approach. We took that as reassuring rather than disappointing. If the agents had invented something wildly idiosyncratic, our first assumption would have been that something had gone wrong.

Where it gets more interesting is the specific choices inside that shape. The agents made a lot of small decisions that a human team would have made differently, and some of those we pushed back on during the meetings. The human scientist in the loop was doing real work there. That's the part people sometimes skip past when they describe this as autonomous. It wasn't.

On the designs themselves, I'd resist strong claims in either direction. We don't have the counterfactual. Nobody ran a matched human team on the same problem with the same time budget, and that experiment would be expensive and still confounded by which particular humans you picked. What we can say is that the outputs were plausible, they were testable, and a subset held up when tested. That's a much weaker statement than "better than humans," and I think the honest framing is that we demonstrated a workflow can produce real candidates, not that we established a comparison.

The value I'd actually point to is different from novelty anyway. It's throughput and documentation. The agents generated and triaged far more candidates than a small human team would have patience for, and every decision was logged with a stated rationale. You can go back and read why something was dropped. That's rare in practice, and it makes the whole thing auditable in a way that human lab meetings usually aren't.

If I were designing the study again, I'd try to get at the counterfactual more directly. Give human teams and agent teams the same target and the same constraints, and compare not just the hit rate but the diversity of what each explored. My suspicion is that the agents are more thorough and less inspired, and humans are the reverse. But that's a hypothesis, and I'd rather say it's a hypothesis than dress it up as a finding.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a difficult counterfactual to establish. You’d ideally give a human team the same starting information, the same tools, and a comparable budget, and then compare what they produce. And you’d want to compare both the experimental performance of the nanobodies and the decisions along the way: which approaches they considered, what they tested, and how they revised their designs.

I would also separate two questions. One is whether a human expert could have proposed a particular design or workflow. The other is whether a team would actually have arrived at it under those constraints. Those are quite different. A workflow can look reasonable in retrospect without being the one you would have chosen beforehand.

So experimental success alone wouldn’t establish that the Virtual Lab did something humans couldn’t do. It would establish that it produced useful designs. To make a stronger claim about how it compares with human teams, we’d need that direct comparison.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a hard counterfactual to establish. We can look at the designs and ask human experts whether they’re reasonable, but that doesn’t tell us whether those experts would have arrived at the same designs independently.

There are really two questions: would a human team choose a similar workflow, and would it produce nanobodies with similar experimental performance? To assess that rigorously, you’d want to give a human team and the Virtual Lab the same starting information, the same constraints, and comparable experimental budgets, then evaluate their candidates side by side. You’d also want to track the time and expert effort involved.

So I would be cautious about claiming that humans couldn’t have come up with these designs. The more useful question is whether the Virtual Lab can help us get to experimentally useful candidates with less time and effort, and whether it adds value to what human scientists can do.
